title: Tenant Capacity Profiling, Cost Prediction, and QBR Template
author: Asha Patel
content:
Overview

This document describes the standardized approach Redwood Customer Success (CS) and SRE use to: 1) profile an enterprise tenant’s capacity and request shape, 2) produce a 3–12 month cost and capacity prediction for QBRs, and 3) include a reusable QBR template that surfaces risk, recommended actions, and contractual implications for Dedicated/Private customers. The goal is to make capacity conversations data-driven and reproducible across accounts.

Goals
- Provide a canonical set of metrics and queries for tenant-level capacity profiling.
- Define a lightweight forecasting methodology (short, medium, long horizon) that balances observed telemetry with business signals.
- Produce a QBR-ready one-pager and supporting appendix for technical stakeholders and commercial owners.
- Define ownership, cadence, and escalation steps when capacity risk exceeds thresholds.

Scope
- Applies to: Dedicated and Private tenants, customers with committed capacity contracts, and any Hosted customer requesting formal capacity planning.
- Not covered: model training costs, third-party model hosting (unless integrated through Redwood routing), or non-inference infrastructure (storage-only pipelines).

Definitions and Key Metrics
- 95th/99th P90/P99 Latency: token-level generation latency at the configured model route.
- Token-throughput (tokens/s): measured per model pool.
- Requests per second (RPS): API request rate.
- Concurrency: number of simultaneous in-flight requests per tenant.
- Tail utilization: percent of time a tenant consumes >80% of its reserved GPU pool.
- Cost-per-1k-tokens: unit-cost metric normalized for forecasting.

Primary Data Sources (examples)\- Metrics: telemetry ingestion (Prometheus) -> metric names: redwood.request.count, redwood.request.latency_ms, redwood.kv_cache.hit_rate, redwood.tokens.generated
- Billing: per-tenant billing records (BigQuery table: billing.tenant_usage)
- Traces: sampled request traces in X-Ray/Jaeger for degradation analysis
- Config: tenant_config table for reserved pool sizes, routing policies, model pins

Profiling Methodology (step-by-step)
1) Baseline window: collect a 14-day rolling window and a 90-day window to surface seasonality.
2) Slice by route/model: generate per-route metrics (latency, tokens/s, RPS).
3) Identify burst patterns: compute 5-min and 1-hour rolling percentiles to detect short vs sustained peaks.
4) Compute cost-normalized utilization: join billing.tenant_usage with tokens generated -> compute cost-per-1k-tokens and effective spend distribution.

Example queries (BigQuery / SQL)
- 14-day per-route RPS and P95 latency:

SELECT route,
  COUNT(1)/1400.0 AS rps_avg_per_min,
  APPROX_QUANTILES(latency_ms, 100)[OFFSET(95)] AS p95_latency_ms
FROM telemetry.requests
WHERE tenant_id = "${TENANT_ID}"
  AND ts BETWEEN TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 14 DAY) AND CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
GROUP BY route;

- Cost normalization (simplified):

SELECT tenant_id, SUM(tokens_generated) AS tokens, SUM(billed_amount_usd) AS billed
FROM billing.tenant_usage
WHERE tenant_id = "${TENANT_ID}"
  AND billing_period BETWEEN "2024-01" AND "2024-12"
GROUP BY tenant_id;

Forecasting approach
- Short horizon (0–30 days): exponential smoothing on the 14-day window + incorporate scheduled events (product launches) provided by the customer. Use conservative uplift of observed peaks (x1.25) when unknown.
- Medium horizon (1–3 months): ARIMA-lite with seasonality (weekday vs weekend) applied to daily RPS and tokens. Use contractual ramp if provided.
- Long horizon (3–12 months): scenario-based forecast: low/expected/high using business-reported growth rates and 3x stress overlay for capacity planning.

Quantitative thresholds (operational triggers)
- Yellow: tail utilization > 50% for 6+ hours/day for 3 consecutive days -> CS notified, schedule review.
- Orange: tail utilization > 70% for 12+ hours/day for 2 consecutive days or sudden 2x increase in sustained RPS -> Initiate capacity burst plan and FinOps review.
- Red: tail utilization > 90% for 4+ hours or sustained P99 latency > 2x SLO -> Incident escalation to Eng-SRE and commercial lead; consider immediate autoscale/burst and compensation discussion.

Runbook: When forecast crosses threshold
1) Validate telemetry: confirm data integrity (check missing metrics, agent restarts). Typical checks: Prometheus scrape errors, gap detection in request.count.
2) Verify tenant config: confirm reserved pool size, route pins, and any routing policies that could be diverting load.
3) Short mitigation: enable burst for 72 hours (Dedicated burst policy), temporarily increase concurrency caps, apply model switchover to compatible smaller model.
4) Medium mitigation: schedule capacity re-provisioning request with Eng-SRE; propose revised commit/renewal sizes to customer.
5) Post-event analysis: generate postmortem and update tenant forecast model with new observed parameters.

Communications and Ownership
- CS Owner: primary point for customer comms (owns QBR delivery, business context).
- Eng-SRE Owner: responsible for capacity changes, autoscale parameters, and burst provisioning.
- FinOps Owner: validates cost assumptions and prepares commercial options.
- Escalation path: CS -> Eng-SRE on-call -> Platform Engineering escalations manager -> VP Customer Success for contract-level interventions.

QBR one-pager template (use during quarterly reviews)
1) Executive summary (1–2 sentences): current capacity health, forecast band, and recommended commercial action.
2) Key metrics (table): 30/90/365 day RPS, tokens/month, P95/P99 latency, tail utilization, cost-per-1k-tokens.
3) Forecast snapshot (graph placeholder): expected low/med/high for next 12 months and recommended committed capacity.
4) Risk & mitigation (bulleted): scheduled events, model upgrades, potential multi-region cutover risk.
5) Action items (owner + due date): clear next steps and decision points.

Sample QBR table (text representation)
| Metric | Last 30 days | Last 90 days | Forecast next 90d (median) | Action |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Avg RPS | 12.5 | 9.8 | 15 (median) | Consider +1 reserved GPU 
| Tokens / month | 85M | 72M | 110M | Approve 20% uplift commit
| P95 latency (ms) | 320 | 290 | 340 | Monitor; possible model swap to v2-compact

Operational appendix (artifacts to produce)
- Export: 14 & 90-day CSVs (per-route RPS, tokens, latency).
- Cost model: one-line spreadsheet with unit costs and forecasted monthly spend by scenario.
- Synthetic test runs: 3 synthetic journeys (typical, burst, adversarial) with expected latency targets and pass/fail.

Synthetic test example (k6 CLI pseudo)
- Command: k6 run --vus 200 --duration 5m synthetic-journey.js --tenant ${TENANT_ID}
- Pass criteria: median latency < 500ms, 95th < 1.5x SLO for the route.

Commercial guidance and decision matrix
- If forecasted median spend exceed committed spend by <15% -> recommend short-term burst + FinOps review.
- If forecasted median spend exceed committed spend by 15–35% -> propose contract amendment or tiered burst schedule.
- If forecasted median spend exceed committed spend by >35% or sustained tail utilization in Orange/Red -> escalate to Sales/Legal for SLA amendment and potential credits.

Template delivery checklist (before QBR)
1) Generate profiling CSVs and forecast scenarios.
2) Run synthetic journeys and attach results.
3) Prepare one-pager QBR and internal appendix.
4) CS reviews with customer 7 days prior; collect product launch dates or known events.
5) Present QBR; capture decisions and convert to action items in the customer Jira board.

Appendix: Quick diagnostic checklist (for CS on-call)
- Are Prometheus scrapes healthy for tenant metrics? (yes/no)
- Is there a sudden change in request.size distribution? (investigate payload changes)
- Is KV cache hit rate degraded? (if < 25% for model routes, consider cache warm-up)
- Any model switch or deployment in the last 48 hours? (check release-notes)
